stem: Suresh starts from point P. He walks 5 km North, then turns and walks 12 km East to reach point Q. What is the straight-line distance from P to Q?

per_option_rationale.rationale: North and East are perpendicular; distance = sqrt(5^2 + 12^2) = sqrt(25+144) = sqrt(169) = 13 km.
17 = 5 + 12, the total path length; this adds legs instead of applying Pythagoras.
11 = 12 - 1 or comes from subtracting legs rather than using the Pythagorean formula.
15 = sqrt(225) would require 9^2+12^2 or 9+12, a slip substituting 9 for 5 in the formula.

explanation: North and East are perpendicular directions. The route forms a right triangle with legs 5 and 12. The straight-line distance PQ is the hypotenuse: sqrt(5^2+12^2) = sqrt(169) = 13 km. The 5-12-13 Pythagorean triple is worth memorising.

explanation_sections.punchline: A classic 5-12-13 right triangle: sqrt(25+144)=sqrt(169)=13 km.
explanation_sections.approach: Deductive trace: identify that North and East are perpendicular, forming a right triangle. Legs are 5 and 12. Hypotenuse = sqrt(5^2+12^2) = 13. The triple 5-12-13 can be verified: 25+144=169=13^2.
explanation_sections.lesson: Memorise common Pythagorean triples (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17); in direction problems, whenever two legs are perpendicular, straight-line distance = hypotenuse.
explanation_sections.timing: 30-40 seconds. The trap is adding 5+12=17 (option 2). Recognising the 5-12-13 triple eliminates all computation.
